Why is oil price not simply Brent?

Not so long ago, people used the word 'oil prices' loosely to describe everything from crude oil to diesel to gasoline. That wasn't necessarily wrong either since the prices tracked each other closely.

Slowly, refining capacity in the world declined. Some mega refineries got built in the Middle East, China and Africa, while the smaller, older outfits were rationalized, many in the Atlantic Basin. 

Then came the US-Iran war. Middle Eastern refineries suffered strikes and could not resume normal operations quickly. Asian refineries suffered loss of feedstock due to the Strait of Hormuz closure but eventually diversified their crude slate to run up to max. However refineries in China were curtailed in production by government-mandated product export quotas.

The crisis further compounded when Ukraine started attacking Russian refineries relentless with drones. 

All these resulted in refining capacity shortages. When refining is constrained, it results in a blowout of product cracks, which is the spread between product and crude. Lo and behold, 'oil prices' cannot be used interchangeably anymore and we have to differentiate between crude oil (Brent) and diesel or mogas prices.

So if we see flatprice coming off, we are not necessarily going to see diesel or gasoline prices coming off in the same way in the current environment we are in. Refining capacity is expected to remain constrained until either Russia, China and/or the Middle Eastern refineries start running again at higher throughput, or demand destruction happens in a large scale.

And don't forget that exorbitant freight rate plaguing the markets which increases the price of crude delivered into the refineries. The product prices will need to factor in the entire cost of input, not just flatprice!

Until then, be more explicit with which 'oil price' you are referring to. We are far from the good old days.

#oott

Over the past decade, energy has been the sector where you throw your career away. For those of us who survived, the numerous battle scars can fill a bookshelf. I can’t count how many times I thought about quitting. You can read through the archive in the “memo” tab to get a glimpse of the pain we all had to go through.

But now that energy is front and center in the global investing landscape, most people are still choosing to ignore it because it’s transitory. IEA, the energy agency created to help the world avoid an oil shortage, continues to blatantly publish reports that sound like propaganda pieces.

“We will be fine,” it says.

All you have to do is compare its forward oil deficit projections today with what it published in June. Another quarter went by; it revised the deficits higher, changed the Q4 2026 surplus into a deficit, and then continued to forecast a 2027 surplus.

Seriously, that’s not analysis. That’s Excel drag on steroids.

And although this kind of stuff gets on my nerves, as you can probably tell from the tone of this memo, it still gives me hope that the worst is ahead of us. It’s usually never a good thing when IEA panics, because when it does, it’s probably the time to sell everything.

This won’t work for many reasons. First of all, it would put money directly into the hands of folks associated with the IRGC. Secondly, most of these >20yo rust buckets are too old to be allowed into ports and would not pass a safety inspection. Thirdly, if the oil isn’t loaded directly at a port, an STS transfer involving a legitimate tanker would only put that tanker on the tracking systems’ naughty lists.

And then there’s the matter of tankers being blacklisted by multiple sanctioning authorities, such as the EU, UK, Switzerland, Ukraine, etc. Those countries could still take their own actions, as we saw France do a couple of days ago. The Dark Fleet vessels themselves are not the solution, but their crews would be, given their insights into and experience with moving oil on behalf of the IRGC. They are the best asset squeeze out of the Dark Fleet, especially as tankers are being hit continuously in the SoH.

Recent Trades & A Few Thoughts… Would love to get some feedback from the physic guys on my half baked thesis. Our desk is hopelessly split on this right now, and frankly i'm losing the plot.

Quick recap of my recent trades for context. As many of you know, I printed solid gains in precious and crypto over the summer, but got completely butchered on the long duration trade in September.

Trump and Bessent just sat on the sidelines watching as spectators, and my entire thesis collapsed right along with "that goddamn house." Swallowing my disgust, I bought bonds for the first time in five years—only to prove the age old market adage that "just bc something looks cheap doesn't make it good". Zero excuses on my end.

Then in late September, watching several late followers jump on the bandwagon way after the fact regarding the uptick in Hormuz transit, I started bidding crude. I fully topped up my position on October 2nd following "Macaron’s" SPR release announcement: https://t.co/J52Iw6Rtwm

Right now i'm locking in some profits and rolling the book. Took off most of my Dec Brent calls that I’d been sitting on for months, and took profit on prompt WTI futures added in late September before rolling them over.

On Tuesday, seeing the Brent-WTI spread invert, I initiated shorts across a few tanker names. Since it was purely tactical, I covered a portion today. Here’s my working thesis on the WTI rally and the pullback in tanker freight:

1) Tankers are trickling out of the Middle East toward the Atlantic, which cools down freight rates. As the freight drag weighing on Americas and WAF physic diffs eases up, Atlantic barrels stage a broad rebound.

In Brent, as WTI Midland cargoes clear the North Sea Platts Window, the super tightening in Dated Brent begins to unwind. Given that the NSea Nov loading program doesn’t look particularly tight, physic diffs should soften into late October/early November.

This in turn starts supporting refinery margins, which had been crushed by exorbitant physic diffs and freight (quick reminder: real refinery margins factoring in landed costs are far uglier than headline cracks suggest—diesel crack is basically the only thing keeping the lights on).

Why are tankers ballasting back to the Atlantic, even in small numbers? Two lines of thought:

1-1) Iran is stepping up attacks in the Strait, and the US midterms are right around the corner.

Liftings could theoretically be down, though recent NOC tender activity out of the Gulf suggests otherwise. If that's the case, shipowners may finally be pricing in physical kinetic threats and shying away from the Middle East. 

Rather than risk a vessel in this high margin tape, they might opt for longer haul Atlantic voyages—less lucrative than Gulf runs, but still plenty profitable on a risk adjusted basis.

1-2) STS capacity is redlining.

Putting the Gulf of Oman aside, Hormuz shuttle tanker capacity is strictly finite, and Saudi tapping into this network has triggered a severe bottleneck. 

Transshipments are dragging out—some vessels are now chalking up over five separate STS legs just to hit their final discharge port. With demurrage stacking up and voyages turning into logistical deadweight, owners may simply be bypassing the Middle East altogether and rerouting to the Atlantic.

2) I personally doubt it, but freight rates themselves could just be peaking. Looking at the blown out spread between LR2 and MR earnings, clean-dirty switching looks pretty aggressive right now.

Coupled with that switching, rumors of Washington weighing sanctions relief on Russian-linked crude tankers might be dragging freight down. 

That said even if sanctions are lifted tomorrow, it’s not like the entire ghost fleet immediately resumes mainstream service—many are already moving Urals anyway, so the marginal supply impact should be negligible.

Besides this peak-freight angle directly contradicts the oil glut bros preaching "more flows, more cargo"—after all tanker demand is a direct function of crude supply. I’m no shipping specialist, so I’ll leave that to the shipping desks to judge.

Bottom line: I’m leaning toward case 1-1, but the tape needs to validate it. 

Over the next 2–3 weeks, we need empirical confirmation that loadings or transits out of the Middle East are actually taking a hit. If recent Iranian strikes knock even 2–3 mb/d out of Hormuz flows, this whole puzzle snaps right into place.

Either way here is the net effect as I see it:

- Prevents refinery run cuts

- US commercial crude draws and a bid back into the WTI structure

- Dated Brent softens

- Headline crack spreads compress, but realized refinery netbacks might actually bounce, with crude quality mismatches eventually forcing diesel cracks higher again.

- Crude starts clawing back the margin share previously monopolized by diesel and freight

What else am I missing here? Head's spinning from all the moving parts, so fire away with your thoughts.

#oott #iran

text:
What a wild ride in US Treasuries yesterday. A heavily oversold market, combined with a bout of weakness in tech stocks, was enough to trigger a sharp yield reversal. 

As my colleague put it in today's Quick Take:
US treasury yields swung wildly on the release of the hot US September CPI data, first spiking higher and with the yield curve flattening as the benchmark 2-year yield rose as much as 16 basis points before getting crushed lower as weak risk sentiment across the board saw a strong bid in the treasury market, sending yields back to unchanged on the day and then lower still early Thursday. The benchmark 2-year yield is near 4.73%, down five basis points from Wednesday’s starting point. At the longer end of the yield curve, the 10-year treasury yield rose 12 basis points after the US CPI data but then fully erased that moved and then some early Thursday, trading below 5.11%, down more than ten basis points from where it opened the prior day and suddenly at a three-week low.
